data.summary: Education is the systematic process through which learning, knowledge, skills, values and habits are acquired, and it is broader than schooling: it is a lifelong journey of personal and social development. It is commonly classified as formal, non-formal and informal, each with a distinct setting and purpose. Education also has a humanity dimension, since it should build empathy, ethical reasoning and social responsibility rather than produce only job-ready skills, and it carries intellectual, moral, social and economic goals. In Nepal the system has moved from the traditional gurushekha system to modern schooling, with the National Education Plan 2019 stressing inclusive, equitable and quality education for all.
importantConcepts: Education as a lifelong process rather than schooling
The four goals of education: intellectual, moral, social and economic
Education and humanity: empathy, ethics and social responsibility
Nepal's shift from gurushekha to modern schooling
National Education Plan 2019: inclusive, equitable and quality education
importantStatements: Education is the systematic facilitation of learning; schooling is only one part of it.
Formal education is curriculum-based and takes place in schools, colleges and universities.
Non-formal education is organized but sits outside the formal system, for example adult education and vocational training.
Informal education is unplanned lifelong learning from family, peers, media and everyday experience.
When education becomes purely job-oriented it risks producing skilled but morally empty individuals.
The National Education Plan 2019 in Nepal emphasizes inclusive, equitable and quality education for all.
importantTasks: Define education and explain why it is not the same as schooling.
Distinguish formal, non-formal and informal education with an example of each.
Discuss the role of education in nation-building.
Explain how education contributes to the development of human values.
State the four goals of education and give an example of each in the Nepali context.
keyPoints: Formal: structured, curriculum-based learning in an institution.
Non-formal: organized learning outside the formal system, such as vocational or adult education.
Informal: learning from family, peers, media and everyday experience.
Goals: intellectual, that is critical thinking and creativity; moral, that is character and ethical judgment; social, that is cooperation and civic duty; and economic, that is employment.
True education nurtures humanity through empathy, ethical reasoning and social responsibility.
Nepal: gurushekha to modern schooling, with the National Education Plan 2019 guiding inclusive and equitable education.
specialNotes: Informal education is not the absence of education; it is highly influential in shaping attitudes, values and behaviour.
Non-formal education is organized and intentional but does not follow the formal curriculum or award the same degrees.
Do not confuse the duration of education with its type: an adult literacy class is non-formal, not informal.
The distinction matters because informal learning shapes character while formal learning shapes qualifications and skills.
examShortTricks: Curriculum means formal, organized but no curriculum means non-formal, and no plan at all means informal.
For a difference question, answer under the headings setting, purpose and outcome instead of one long sentence.
Memorize one Nepali example for each type: a school for formal, a vocational training centre for non-formal, and learning from parents for informal.
examNotes: Define education and give its types is the most frequently set question in this unit.
The difference between formal and informal education is commonly a two- or three-mark question.
MCQs often test the idea that education is broader than schooling, and the four goals of education.
For role-of-education questions, connect to nation building, citizenship and social responsibility, not only to jobs.
practiceQuestions: Define education. Why can it not be equated with schooling?
Differentiate between formal and informal education with examples.
What are the goals of education in a democratic society?
How does education contribute to nation-building?
Describe any one change from the gurushekha system to modern schooling in Nepal.

mcs.question: Education is best described as
options: A lifelong systematic process of learning
mcs.explanation: Education includes formal, non-formal and informal learning and continues throughout life, whereas schooling is only one part of it.

mcs.question: Vocational training run by an institute outside the school system is
mcs.explanation: It is organized and intentional but lies outside the formal school system, which makes it non-formal education.

mcs.question: Learning values and manners from parents and elders is
mcs.explanation: It is unplanned, lifelong learning from family and society, so it is informal education.

mcs.question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of education?
mcs.explanation: Economic preparation is one goal, but education aims at intellectual, moral and social development as well, so earning money alone is not a complete goal.

mcs.question: The National Education Plan 2019 of Nepal emphasizes
options: Inclusive, equitable and quality education for all
mcs.explanation: The plan stresses inclusion, equity and quality so that every child can access education of good standard.
